concept.technique_name: subject-verb pair test for sentence fragments

examples.problem_statement: Answer (A) repeats the original sentence; choose the version with correct sentence structure. Original: The computer science instructor assigned a new textbook focused on recent advances in artificial intelligence. (A) The computer science instructor assigned a new textbook focused on recent advances in artificial intelligence. (B) A new textbook that is focused on recent advances in artificial intelligence assigned by our instructor.

solution.operation: In choice (A), locate the subject and its verb: subject = instructor, verb = assigned
solution.description: Check the original sentence first: pick out the noun doing the action and the working verb attached to it, and confirm they pair up.

solution.operation: In choice (B), locate every verb: the only verb is is, which sits inside the dependent clause that ... intelligence
solution.result: (B) has no main verb, so it is a fragment
solution.description: Scan the alternative for verbs. Its single verb is trapped in a dependent clause, which leaves the main clause verbless and makes the sentence a fragment.

solution.operation: Note the repair for (B): insert was before assigned, giving a textbook ... was assigned
solution.result: Adding was turns the modifier into a working verb, confirming (B) as written is broken
solution.description: Confirm the diagnosis by seeing what (B) would need: supplying was makes assigned a real main verb, which shows the printed version lacks one.

solution.operation: Select the choice that already has a main verb
solution.description: Since only (A) contains a complete subject-verb pair in the main clause, it is the correct answer.

key_reminders: Every complete sentence needs a subject paired with a main verb outside any dependent clause.
A verb inside a that-clause belongs to that clause and cannot serve as the sentence's main verb.
A past participle such as assigned is a modifier, not a verb, until a helping verb like was is added.
common_mistakes: Treating is in that is focused on recent advances as the sentence's main verb in choice (B).
Reading assigned by our instructor in (B) as a working verb phrase rather than a modifier of textbook.

concept.technique_name: sentence-clue matching for text completion blanks

examples.problem_statement: Select one entry for each blank from the corresponding column of choices; fill all blanks in the way that best completes the text. In his initial works, the playwright made physical disease (i) ______ factor in the action; from this, his early critics inferred that he had a predilection for focusing on (ii) ______ subject matter. Blank (i): A a pivotal, B a nonexistent, C an obscure. Blank (ii): D recondite, E uncomplicated, F morbid.

solution.operation: Interpret the phrase a predilection for focusing on: a writer with such a predilection makes that thing prominent in the work
solution.result: Blank (i) must mean prominent or significant
solution.description: Read the clue in the second half of the sentence. Because the critics infer a predilection, disease must have been made prominent, which fixes the meaning Blank (i) has to carry.

solution.operation: Match prominent or significant against A a pivotal, B a nonexistent, C an obscure
solution.description: Test each Blank (i) option against the required meaning; only pivotal expresses prominence, so it is selected.

solution.operation: Determine what Blank (ii) must describe: the subject matter of physical disease
solution.result: Blank (ii) needs a word characterizing disease as subject matter
solution.description: Identify the referent for the second blank. The critics are characterizing the playwright's focus on physical disease, so the word must describe that content.

solution.operation: Match that requirement against D recondite, E uncomplicated, F morbid
solution.description: Compare the Blank (ii) options to a description of disease as subject matter; morbid is the choice that fits.

examples.answer: Choice A: a pivotal; Choice F: morbid

key_reminders: The word for a blank must be supported by an explicit clue elsewhere in the sentence.
A predilection for focusing on something implies that thing is prominent in the work.
Each blank is answered from its own column of choices.
common_mistakes: Choosing B a nonexistent for Blank (i), which contradicts the critics' inference that the playwright dwelt on disease.
Choosing D recondite for Blank (ii) by matching the tone of obscure rather than the actual subject matter, physical disease.

concept.technique_name: Sunyam Sam Samuchchaya sutra for rational-to-quadratic equations

examples.problem_statement: Using the Quadratic Equations via Vedic Mathematics technique (Sunyam Sam Samuchchaya sutra, which gives two routes to the roots based on numerator-denominator relationships), solve \frac{3x+6}{6x+3} = \frac{5x+4}{2x+7} and state both roots.

solution.result: A rational equation that reduces to a quadratic
solution.description: Label the two numerators and two denominators so the sutra's conditions can be tested; recognise the equation as a rational one that simplifies to a quadratic.
Add the numerators and add the denominators; they come out equal, so the first condition of the sutra is satisfied and its shortcut applies.

solution.operation: Set N_1 + N_2 = 0: \; 8x+10 = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; x = -\frac{5}{4}
solution.description: Because the sums are equal, the sutra lets you set that common sum to zero; solving the resulting linear equation delivers the first root immediately.

solution.operation: Apply the second condition: N_1 - D_1 = N_2 - D_2 = 0
solution.result: A second equation supplied by the sutra
solution.description: Move to the sutra's other route: form the numerator-minus-denominator differences and set them to zero to obtain the remaining root.
Subtract the first denominator from the first numerator and set the difference to zero, then solve the linear equation for x.
Repeat the subtraction on the second fraction as a check; it yields the same value, confirming the second root.

solution.operation: Collect the roots from both routes: x = -\frac{5}{4}, \; x = 1
solution.description: Gather the results of the two conditions and confirm they are consistent, giving both roots of the quadratic.

examples.answer: The two roots are x = -5/4 and x = 1, found using Sunyam Sam Samuchchaya sutra with conditions N1+N2 = D1+D2 and N1-D1 = N2-D2.

key_reminders: Sunyam Sam Samuchchaya: when N_1+N_2 equals D_1+D_2, that common sum may be set to zero to give a root.
The second route applies when N_1-D_1 equals N_2-D_2; setting that difference to zero gives the other root.
Both conditions must be verified on the actual expressions before the shortcut is used.
common_mistakes: Cross-multiplying and expanding the quadratic instead of noticing that N_1+N_2 and D_1+D_2 are both 8x+10.
Sign slips when forming (3x+6)-(6x+3) = -3x+3, which flips the root away from x = 1.

concept.technique_name: out-of-order blank filling using logical connectors

examples.problem_statement: Select one entry for each blank from the corresponding column of choices; fill all blanks in the way that best completes the text. Repression of painful memories is sometimes called “willed forgetting.” Yet true forgetting is (i) ______ than the phenomenon of repressed memory. In spite of the effort that it (ii) ______, repressing unwanted memories is less (iii) ______ than truly forgetting them, for repressed memories are prone to come back. Blank (i): A less controlled, B different in its effect, C far more common. Blank (ii): D eases, E conveys, F entails. Blank (iii): G permanent, H arduous, I immediate.

solution.operation: Start with Blank (iii): the word for indicates that repressed memories are prone to come back is the basis of the comparison
solution.result: Blank (iii) must relate to the tendency of memories to come back
solution.description: Do not work left to right. The connector for marks the final clause as the evidence for the third blank, so tackle that blank first.

solution.operation: Test G permanent, H arduous, I immediate against the tendency to come back
solution.description: Compare each Blank (iii) option with the stated evidence; only permanent bears on whether memories return, so it is selected.

solution.operation: Work backward to Blank (ii): the clause opens with In spite of, so the blank must set up an expectation contrary to what follows
solution.result: Blank (ii) must express that repressing costs effort, since effort would ordinarily make something more permanent
solution.description: Use the concessive opener. In spite of demands that the blank create an expectation the sentence then overturns, and one expects effort to yield more permanence, not less.

solution.operation: Test D eases, E conveys, F entails against that requirement
solution.description: Eliminate the Blank (ii) options that set up no such expectation; neither eases nor conveys does, leaving entails.

solution.operation: With blanks (ii) and (iii) filled, evaluate Blank (i) options A less controlled, B different in its effect, C far more common against the completed text
solution.result: Choice B, different in its effect
solution.description: Return to the first blank last. Nothing in the finished text supports more common or less controlled, but the text does establish that true forgetting differs in effect by being more permanent.

examples.answer: Choice B: different in its effect; Choice F: entails; Choice G: permanent

key_reminders: Fill the blank with the strongest textual clue first, not necessarily the first blank.
The connector for introduces the reason or evidence supporting the preceding claim.
In spite of signals that the expectation set up by the clause is about to be reversed.
common_mistakes: Choosing C far more common for Blank (i), a comparison the passage never supports.
Choosing H arduous for Blank (iii), which repeats the effort idea already carried by Blank (ii) instead of matching the come-back evidence.
Choosing D eases for Blank (ii), which removes the effort that In spite of requires.
